title: When a computer filled a room
alt: People work among tall IBM 7090 cabinets and consoles in a NASA computer room around 1962.
caption: NASA’s computer room with two IBM 7090s, around 1962. Large shared computers made scheduling, storage and device management essential. Early batch systems queued jobs; time-sharing systems let several people interact with a machine through terminals. This photo shows the hardware and operators, not a particular OS screen.
question: Which parts of this room now fit inside a laptop? Why would a shared computer need to manage whose program runs next?
license: Public domain in the United States (NASA)

title: A terminal becomes a doorway
alt: Ken Thompson seated at a terminal while Dennis Ritchie stands beside him at Bell Labs in 1973.
caption: Ken Thompson (seated) and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1973, several years after Unix began in 1969. Unix helped establish the command-oriented working environment behind many tools we still use. Directories, processes and small cooperating programs made text commands powerful. The original archival image is small; enlarging it cannot reveal extra detail.
question: Where is the keyboard? Where might the actual computer be? How does this compare with the practice terminal in this lesson?
credit: Unknown photographer; via the Jargon File and Wikimedia Commons

title: The command line reaches the desktop
alt: An IBM PC 5150 with a keyboard, two floppy disk drives and a green monochrome monitor displaying DOS text.
caption: The IBM PC model introduced in 1981 helped bring command-driven personal computing into offices and homes. This later photograph shows a preserved machine running MS-DOS 5.0, not its original 1981 software. DOS users typed commands to run programs and manage files. Windows 1.0 arrived in 1985 as a graphical environment extending MS-DOS; today’s Windows is a much later OS family.
question: Find the disk drives and text display. What would you need to know before opening a file without clickable icons?

title: Point, click and open a window
alt: A compact Macintosh 128K photographed against a removed background, showing its built-in screen and floppy disk drive.
caption: The 1984 Macintosh helped popularize mouse-driven graphical computing. Its early system software presented familiar ideas such as windows, icons and a desktop. It was not the first graphical computer, and its classic system software is different from modern macOS. A separate keyboard and mouse (not shown in this photo) let users type and select visible targets instead of remembering every command.
question: Which actions in Finder still use the desktop metaphor? What can a picture communicate more quickly than a typed command?
credit: All About Apple museum; source edits by TDS and Grm wnr / Wikimedia Commons

title: An operating system built in the open
alt: Linus Torvalds seated on the left during an on-stage discussion at LinuxCon North America in 2016.
caption: Linus Torvalds began the Linux kernel in 1991; this discussion photograph was taken much later, at LinuxCon in 2016. A kernel is the core that manages hardware and processes. A usable Linux distribution combines it with system tools, applications and often a graphical desktop. Linux is Unix-like, rather than a copy of the original Unix source code.
question: Why do Ubuntu and Fedora look different even though both use Linux? Which part is the kernel and which part is the desktop?
